title: Justice
hook: do justly (Micah 6:8) in one place you can
tomorrow: Nia asks Grace, "be honest: was my speech bad?" what does she say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, citizenship: captives told to seek Babylon's peace. Your line was seek the city's peace. Today, what makes a city fair.
screen: `SEEK THE CITY'S PEACE.` → `WHAT MAKES IT FAIR?`

segments.voice: A pothole on one street keeps wrecking tires. You could help each driver change a flat, or you could get the city to fix the hole. Christians argue, warmly, over which of those justice mostly is. Both sides quote the same line from the prophet Micah: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” Today, both sides get to speak.
screen: `CHANGE THE TIRE, OR FIX THE HOLE?` → `DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY.` → `BOTH SIDES SPEAK.`

segments.voice: One view starts with hands. In Jesus' story of the Samaritan, nobody repairs the Jericho road. One man stops, binds up a stranger's wounds, and pays the innkeeper. On this view, justice is mostly mercy up close: the meal, the covered shift, the person right in front of you. Rules change; a neighbor who stops is what lasts. The other view starts with the road. Amos cries: “let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” Isaiah says: “seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.” That's courts, wages, rules that crush people quietly. On this view, helping one person at a time while the hole stays open isn't enough. Proverbs adds: “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.” Each side has a best case, and each can see something the other might miss. Micah keeps them in one sentence: do justly, and love mercy, side by side. And today's practice is small enough for either side: one fairness, in one place you can reach.
screen: `HANDS: THE SAMARITAN STOPS.` · `THE ROAD: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN.` · `OPEN THY MOUTH FOR THE POOR.` · `JUSTICE AND MERCY, ONE SENTENCE.` · then, large: `DO JUSTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of one unfairness you can actually reach: a chore that always lands on the same person, a classmate always left out, a schedule that keeps hitting one coworker. Name the fair outcome you want, name what will stop you, and decide your first move: when that happens, I'll do this. If you pray, ask for courage for that one move.
Justice. Making things right for people, by the hand that helps and the voice that changes the rule.
The line to keep: do justly, right beside the mercy, in one place you can reach. That's day 1732.

howItsDone: Christians work for justice in different ways: food banks and shelters, legal aid, prison ministry, and speaking up for fair laws and wages; churches differ on how much to stress each.

myth: Micah asks for mercy instead of justice
do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly: all three in one line.
Christians all agree whether justice means charity or changing rules
some start with hands, like the Samaritan; others with the road, like Amos.

fork.setup: you run the school food drive. your friend says food drives are band-aids and only changing the rules counts. what is her best case, in her own terms?
options: Amos: let judgment run down as waters. if the rules keep making hunger, fix those too.
she just doesn't want to do the work of running a food drive.
the Samaritan story proves that helping one person is pointless.
fork.reveal: her steelman is Amos and Isaiah: justice for the whole road. yours is the Samaritan who stopped. Micah keeps both in one sentence.

original.note: Hebrew: justice, judgment, what's right. 'to do justly' in Micah 6:8 is to do mishpat.

trapdoor: what you thought: justice means punishing bad people.
what it means: making things right for people, both with hands that help and with fair rules for the road.
what a scholar hears: mishpat is what Micah asks people to do, and what Amos wants to run down like water, paired there with righteousness.
guess: making things right for people, hands and rules
punishment that matches the wrongdoer's crime
keeping out of other people's business

chat.says: luis gets stuck closing every night. nia says report the schedule. i'd rather just cover him. who's right?
options: Maybe both: cover one shift, and raise the pattern kindly. Micah wants justice and mercy.
You. Reporting things only makes trouble; quiet kindness is all the Bible asks.
Nia. Covering shifts is a band-aid, and band-aids never count as real justice.
chat.meaning: Micah puts do justly and love mercy in one sentence. Helping Luis and fixing the schedule aren't rivals; each side sees what the other misses.

Micah.meaning: a prophet of Israel; a short Bible book bears his name

Amos.meaning: a prophet of Israel who spoke out for the poor

Samaritan.meaning: in Jesus' story, the outsider who stopped to help

Jericho.meaning: a town; the road in Jesus' story ran down to it

Isaiah.meaning: a prophet of Israel; a long Bible book bears his name

notes: New v3 script (no earlier draft). v3 debate shape: two real emphases inside the tradition (justice as mercy up close; justice as fair structures), each with its best case; the fork asks the learner to state the other side's best case. No side ranked; no party, policy or culture-war topic named.
The pothole picture is an illustration, not a claim. 'Christians argue, warmly' is a hedge with no count.
Luke 10:30–35 paraphrased ('nobody repairs the Jericho road' is a reading of what the story leaves out, offered as the hands view). Confirm framing.
Micah 6:8 was used on days 1178 and 1198 (year 4) and appears again later in year 5 (1766, 1777); this day's angle is the debate between the two emphases.
